edition.deck: Settler violence in the West Bank, Ukraine’s strained ties with Washington and an escalating drought in southern England lead the evening’s coverage.
edition.editorialNote: Prioritises developments reported today and consequential investigations. Alberta’s vote remains relevant because campaigning is entering its final days; unchanged stories from the morning edition are not carried forward without a fresh development.

content.headline: Israeli settlers attack West Bank olive harvesters and journalist
content.shortHeadline: Settlers attack West Bank olive harvesters and journalist
content.standfirst: Palestinians harvesting olives near Abu Falah were attacked by masked settlers, the BBC witnessed. A Washington Post photographer was among those injured as violence during this year’s harvest intensifies.

image.caption: A burned car after an attack on Palestinian olive harvesters near Turmus Ayya.

sources.originalTitle: Palestinians and US journalist injured by Israeli settlers in West Bank harvest attack
Israeli settlers attack olive farmers and Washington Post journalist in West Bank

segments.body: Masked settlers attacked Palestinians harvesting olives near Abu Falah on Friday, burning cars and trees. A local official told the BBC that 12 Palestinians, including four dual Palestinian American citizens, were injured. Washington Post photographer Heidi Levine was also hurt; she said settlers kicked her while she was reporting.

perspectives.body: The BBC team witnessed settlers moving down towards the harvesters and setting olive trees alight. It reported stones being thrown by settlers and Palestinians, then tear gas fired by Israeli forces; it could not establish who fired live ammunition heard nearby.

segments.title: Violence during the harvest
segments.body: The UN says attacks by violent settlers in the first two weeks of this year’s harvest already outnumbered those during the whole of last year’s season. The Guardian, citing the Israeli rights group Yesh Din, reports at least 170 attacks since 27 September; Palestinian authorities say four Palestinians were killed and more than 100 injured over the past month.

segments.title: Restrictions and response
segments.body: The Guardian reports that new Israeli military rules bar Palestinians from harvesting about 8,800 hectares of land in Area C without approval—30% more land than last year. The Israeli military said it had sent personnel after reports of a violent confrontation and would examine the circumstances. The US State Department called for investigations and convictions of those responsible for criminal violence.

content.headline: Trump attacks Zelensky as EU leaders rally behind Ukraine
content.shortHeadline: Trump rebukes Zelensky as EU leaders rally behind Ukraine
content.standfirst: Donald Trump called Ukraine’s renewed strikes on Russian oil refineries “a disgrace” and said Volodymyr Zelensky was harder to deal with than Vladimir Putin. At a Brussels summit, European leaders voiced support for Kyiv.

image.caption: Kyiv and Kharkiv have faced rolling blackouts and water outages this week.

sources.originalTitle: Zelensky says Ukraine has right to defend itself after Trump calls latest strikes a 'disgrace'
Trump calls Ukraine’s renewed strikes on Russian oil refineries ‘a disgrace’
Korrespondent efter nye Trump-udtalelser: Nu er der snart ingen vej tilbage for Ukraine - og Europa
US senators call for investigation into Ukraine's Starlink restrictions
Attacks on Ukraine’s power plants show Russia has given up on military victory

segments.body: Trump criticised Zelensky after Ukraine resumed strikes on Russian oil infrastructure, following Russian attacks on Ukrainian energy sites during a proposed “energy ceasefire”. Zelensky said Kyiv had paused its attacks for three days but would not continue to do so while Russia kept striking. The Kremlin has said it never agreed to the proposed ceasefire.

segments.title: European backing and pressure on Washington
segments.body: At Friday’s Brussels summit, EU leaders backed Ukraine. The European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, said Russia had not respected the proposed ceasefire and promised a further round of sanctions. Zelensky told European leaders that Ukraine needs at least €70bn from the EU for defence and weapons next year, and said it lacked the money to produce as many drones as it could.

segments.title: Disruption and winter risks
segments.body: The row comes amid concerns over US support. Ukrainian officials say a temporary speed restriction on SpaceX’s Starlink service disrupted drone operations; a bipartisan group of US senators has called for an investigation into whether the Pentagon or its contractors were involved. Separately, the Guardian reports that Russian strikes on power infrastructure could worsen blackouts and water outages in Kyiv this winter; the Ukrainian government has not confirmed specific damage described in that report.

content.headline: Carney makes final pitch for Canadian unity ahead of Alberta vote
content.shortHeadline: Carney urges Alberta to stay in Canada before Monday’s vote
content.standfirst: With Alberta’s separation referendum due on Monday, Mark Carney warned that the outcome is not settled by polling and urged voters to turn out. More than 450,000 have already voted early or by mail.

image.caption: Mark Carney campaigns for Alberta to remain in Canada ahead of Monday’s vote.

sources.originalTitle: Canada PM warns 'stakes are high' as Alberta separation vote nears

segments.body: The Canadian prime minister urged Albertans to vote to remain in Canada at a Calgary rally attended by more than 7,000 people. He called the referendum a high-stakes vote and said turnout would determine the result. More than 450,000 ballots have already been cast early or by mail.

segments.title: Grievances and next steps
segments.body: Separatists argue that federal environmental policies have held back Alberta’s oil and gas industry and that the province contributes more to Canada than it receives. Carney says his government will support Alberta’s energy sector and has proposed fast-tracking a pipeline to the Pacific coast. A vote to start the separation process would not itself make Alberta independent; further legal steps would follow.

content.headline: Pope Leo pictured after lung surgery and cancer diagnosis
content.shortHeadline: Pope Leo appears in first images since lung surgery
content.standfirst: The Vatican released the first pictures of Pope Leo XIV since surgery revealed lung cancer. Doctors say his condition is steadily improving and an X-ray showed good recovery of the operated lung.

image.caption: Pope Leo XIV celebrates Mass at the hospital after lung surgery.

sources.originalTitle: Pope pictured for first time since surgery and cancer diagnosis

segments.body: Pope Leo XIV was pictured celebrating Mass at Rome’s Gemelli Hospital on Friday, the first images released since he underwent lung surgery. The Vatican said tests confirmed lung adenocarcinoma, as suspected before the operation, and that the whole lower lobe of his right lung was removed.

The Vatican said the surgery was successful and had no complications. On Friday, the Pope’s doctors reported a steady improvement in his general condition and said an X-ray showed good recovery of the operated lung. The Pope, 71, thanked hospital staff after celebrating Mass with them.

content.headline: Ship attacks near Strait of Hormuz hit weekly record as oil flows slow
content.shortHeadline: Ship attacks reach record near Strait of Hormuz
content.standfirst: BBC Verify counted 12 reported vessel attacks in and around the Strait of Hormuz in the week to 11 October. Oil shipments through the waterway have also slowed, according to industry data.

sources.originalTitle: Ship attack reports near Hormuz reach record high as oil exports slow

segments.body: Twelve vessels reported being attacked in or around the Strait of Hormuz between 5 and 11 October—the highest weekly total since the US-Israeli war with Iran began, BBC Verify says, using reports from the UK Maritime Trade Operations agency. The count is approximate because reports do not all use the same date convention.

segments.title: Impact on shipping and oil
segments.body: Oil shipments through the strait were about 12.6 million barrels a day on 13 October, down from 15 million at the end of September and a pre-war level of about 17 million, according to Kpler data cited by the BBC. A container ship sank after being struck on Tuesday; its 21 crew were evacuated. Two seafarers from an earlier tanker attack remain missing, a union said.

content.headline: Albania protests spread as demonstrators demand Rama’s resignation
content.shortHeadline: Albania protests continue amid clashes and calls for Rama to quit
content.standfirst: Protests in Tirana entered a fourth day, with demonstrators demanding the prime minister’s resignation over corruption, student conditions and development plans. Clashes and damage to public property have been reported.

image.caption: Riot police stand near demonstrators during an anti-government protest in Tirana.

sources.originalTitle: Albanian protests turn violent: What we know
Ny demonstration i Albanien

segments.body: Demonstrations continued in Tirana on Friday for a fourth consecutive day, according to DR, which cited Reuters. Protesters are demanding Prime Minister Edi Rama’s resignation and calling for better conditions for students, action on corruption and opposition to hotel plans in scenic parts of southern Albania.

segments.title: Clashes and competing accounts
segments.body: DR reports that demonstrators smashed windows and traffic lights and were met by a large police presence. The BBC says protests have spread to several cities and that clashes have involved stones, water cannon, tear gas and batons. Rama has ruled out resigning and said he will not yield to violence.

content.headline: Russian anti-war activists face rising deportations from the West
content.shortHeadline: Russian dissidents face deportation as Western asylum rules tighten
content.standfirst: A BBC investigation documents Russian activists and deserters sent back from the US and Europe, where they say they faced interrogation, prosecution or renewed danger. Governments say asylum decisions follow legal standards.

sources.originalTitle: They fled Russia, but the West sent them back

segments.body: Anti-war Russians forcibly returned from Western countries describe being interrogated or threatened with prosecution after arriving home, the BBC reports. One woman, whose name was changed, said Russian security officers questioned her for hours and continue to contact her. A former soldier said he was held in a military detention facility after deportation and later escaped.

segments.title: Falling protection rates
segments.body: The BBC reports that US removals of Russian nationals rose from 222 in 2023 to more than 1,200 in 2025. In Germany, deportations rose from seven in 2023 to more than 110 in 2025, while the proportion of Russian asylum applicants receiving protection in the EU fell. Finnish authorities said their decisions follow international refugee law and that the share granted asylum was in line with EU averages.

content.headline: About 200 people rescued from suspected illegal rehab centre in South Africa
content.shortHeadline: About 200 rescued from suspected illegal South African rehab centre
content.standfirst: Authorities say some patients at a church-run facility in Mpumalanga were chained or living in overcrowded rooms without running water. A pastor and his wife have been charged with kidnapping; more charges may follow.

image.caption: Officials inspect the suspected illegal rehabilitation centre after patients were rescued.

sources.originalTitle: Patients in chains rescued from suspected illegal rehab centre in South Africa

segments.body: Officials found about 200 people at a suspected illegal rehabilitation centre operating from a church in Mpumalanga province. Some patients were chained to one another or had sores, authorities said. A 16-year-old girl and an 11-year-old boy were reportedly held in the same room as adults.

segments.title: Investigation and support
segments.body: Police have charged the pastor and his wife who ran the facility with kidnapping and may add further charges. Fourteen people have been taken to hospital and 132 reunited with their families, police said. One former patient told a local broadcaster that chaining patients was common practice, though he said the centre had helped him overcome addiction.

content.headline: Southern England declared in severe drought as ministers plan response
content.shortHeadline: Severe drought declared across parts of southern England
content.standfirst: Parts of six southern counties are in severe drought for the first time, with more than 4.5 million people in the affected areas. Ministers have discussed contingency measures, though no widespread water rationing is planned.

sources.originalTitle: Car wash bans and low water pressure could hit millions as severe drought declared

segments.body: Severe drought has been declared in parts of Cornwall, Devon, Dorset, Somerset and East and West Sussex after months of below-average rainfall. The status covers areas with more than 4.5 million people. Reservoirs serving customers in West Sussex and Somerset are at their lowest levels for decades.

segments.title: Measures under consideration
segments.body: Ministers and officials met on Thursday to discuss the water supply. The Government is not planning widespread rationing, but water companies may restrict some business use, reduce mains pressure or interrupt supplies in affected areas. Three companies have applied for non-essential-use bans that could affect businesses such as car washes and private pools.

segments.title: What remains uncertain
segments.body: The Environment Agency says households’ supplies will continue uninterrupted and is urging people to conserve water. Reservoir levels may recover if the forecast wetter autumn and winter arrive, but the report notes that heavy rain could also increase flood risk. Water companies have been told to monitor reservoir and river levels daily.

content.headline: Police apologise and pay nine women over handling of abuse allegations
content.shortHeadline: Police force apologises to nine women over abuse investigations
content.standfirst: Devon and Cornwall police settled a claim without admitting liability after women said the force mishandled allegations of abuse by officers. The force says its processes have changed and denies evidence of a cover-up.

sources.originalTitle: UK police force pays out after claims it protected officers accused of abusing women

segments.body: Devon and Cornwall police has apologised to nine women and agreed to pay compensation after a two-year legal battle, the Guardian reports. The women said they experienced abuse including rape, assault, threats and coercive control by male officers, and that the force failed to investigate their reports properly. The settlement was made without an admission of liability.

segments.title: Allegations and the force’s response
segments.body: The women said some alleged abusers were promoted or remained in sensitive roles after complaints, and that investigations were mishandled. The force said the chief constable apologised for the conduct of its investigations, but said no evidence had been identified of a cover-up or misogyny. It says all such allegations will now be investigated by its professional standards department and that it is developing a victim advocate role.

The women’s solicitor said litigation should not have been necessary and described the similarities in the alleged failures as evidence of a broken system. The force was placed into special measures for overall poor performance a fortnight ago, the Guardian reports. It declined to answer whether the accused officers named by the women were still serving.

content.headline: London robotaxi rollout faces protests and calls for stronger oversight
content.shortHeadline: London robotaxis face protests as calls grow for TfL control
content.standfirst: Drivers are planning a protest as autonomous taxi trials expand, while a London Assembly committee says Transport for London should have greater power over permits. The effects on jobs, safety and congestion remain uncertain.

image.caption: Wayve robotaxis leave their London depot for passenger rides via Uber.

sources.originalTitle: ‘We should all be worried’: calls grow to limit London rollout of robotaxis

segments.body: Uber and Wayve’s limited robotaxi service in London, which still uses a human safety driver, is facing opposition from drivers and politicians. Drivers’ union members plan to protest outside Wayve’s headquarters this weekend. Trials also expanded to Manchester this week, and Uber has announced plans for a much larger global robotaxi fleet from next year.

segments.title: Who should regulate the services?
segments.body: A London Assembly transport committee has called for Transport for London to have fuller powers to permit or suspend autonomous taxi operations. Its report says the benefits remain uncertain and raises questions about public transport, congestion, safeguarding and accessibility. Under the current arrangements, the Department for Transport would issue permits for fully autonomous services, with TfL able to grant or refuse consent.

segments.title: Drivers’ concerns and company response
segments.body: Drivers say they fear losing income and point to their role in safeguarding passengers. Wayve says it is taking a phased approach and has worked with local leaders and accessibility groups. Uber says drivers and autonomous vehicles are expected to operate alongside each other for some time, while acknowledging that automation will affect workers and communities.

content.headline: MI5 launches AI threat centre amid warning about potential bioweapons
content.shortHeadline: MI5 opens AI threat centre amid bioweapons warning
content.standfirst: MI5 chief Ken McCallum warned that AI could help less sophisticated actors access dangerous biological knowledge, though he said such a threat has not yet materialised. A new centre will assess the technology’s security risks.

sources.originalTitle: UK at growing risk of terror attack with deadly man-made viruses, warns MI5 boss

segments.body: MI5 has launched an AI Threat Assessment Centre to evaluate risks and opportunities from the technology. Its director general, Ken McCallum, said AI could allow dangerous knowledge to reach terrorists seeking biological or other weapons, but stressed that such a capability had not yet emerged.

segments.title: Wider security concerns
segments.body: McCallum also described Russia as the leading state threat to UK security and said MI5 is devoting more resources to state threats than during the Cold War. He warned that publicly amplifying Russian online activity could help spread division. The agency also reported more than 50 arrests in the UK linked to Iran-related operations over the past year.

content.headline: Defence voices urge faster UK rearmament amid warnings about Russia
content.shortHeadline: Calls grow for faster UK defence spending as Russia threat rises
content.standfirst: Military figures and former ministers say the Government should move faster to fund defence as Russia increases hostile activity. The Chancellor is expected to address a £4.7bn gap in the Defence Investment Plan at this month’s Budget.

sources.originalTitle: The drones and missiles the UK needs to defend itself – and the cuts to pay for them

segments.body: The Government faces a £4.7bn shortfall in its Defence Investment Plan, which Chancellor John Healey is expected to address in his Budget on 28 October. Former ministers and military figures cited by the i Paper argue that further investment is needed to prepare for Russian hybrid activity and potential threats to the UK and its allies.

segments.title: Disagreement over pace and funding
segments.body: Former defence secretary Lord Hutton urged a national rearmament programme and said waiting for the next spending review could be too late. General Sir Richard Barrons said the immediate priority was filling the existing plan’s funding gap and proposed involving private capital. Conservative defence spokesperson James Cartlidge called for a clear timetable to raise defence spending to 3% of GDP by 2030.

The report describes gaps in the UK’s air defences, ammunition stocks and heavy armour, while current plans aim to raise defence spending to 2.7% of GDP next year. These are arguments from the report’s interviewees; the Government’s expected Budget decisions and longer-term spending plans remain unresolved.

content.headline: Woman tells court Russell Brand tried to drag her into toilets
content.shortHeadline: Woman says Brand tried to drag her into toilets, court hears
content.standfirst: A woman told Southwark Crown Court that Russell Brand grabbed her arm and tried to pull her into a men’s toilet in 2001. Brand denies the charges against him, which include rape and sexual assault.

image.caption: Russell Brand leaves Southwark Crown Court during his trial.

sources.originalTitle: Russell Brand was ‘wild-eyed maniac’ when trying to drag woman into toilets, court told

segments.body: A woman who worked at MTV told the court that Brand grabbed her forearm and tried to pull her into the men’s toilets, where he allegedly pleaded with her to come inside. She said she freed herself and later told two colleagues. The alleged incident is part of a trial involving six women and charges spanning 1999 to 2009; Brand denies all the charges.

segments.title: Evidence and defence
segments.body: The woman said she did not report the incident to police until after a 2023 documentary about Brand, because she was afraid of the consequences for her job. In cross-examination, the defence suggested she had reassessed her memory and that Brand had invited her into the toilet; she rejected both suggestions. The court heard earlier testimony from witnesses connected to a separate allegation.

content.headline: Ministers consider replacing under-25s’ health-related benefits with job support
content.shortHeadline: Under-25s could get more job support and less benefits cash
content.standfirst: A reported proposal would replace the health element of universal credit for some under-25s with employment and health support. The plans are not final, and it is not clear whether they would include disability payments.

image.caption: Alan Milburn, whose review is considering support for young people out of work or education.

sources.originalTitle: The new benefits system for Gen Z: Less cash and more job support

segments.body: The i Paper reports that Alan Milburn’s review of youth unemployment may recommend replacing the universal credit health element for under-25s with more intensive health and employment support. Claimants could be required to take up that support to receive benefits. The Government has not confirmed the proposal, and the review’s final report is expected in November.

segments.title: Scale and open questions
segments.body: The Office for National Statistics counted 981,000 people aged 16 to 24 not in education, employment or training between April and June. Milburn’s interim report said 45% of young people in this group reported having a disability. It remains unclear whether the reported proposal would affect personal independence payments or existing claimants.

content.headline: BBC and Government still negotiating a replacement for the licence fee
content.shortHeadline: BBC funding deal faces delay as licence fee talks continue
content.standfirst: The BBC and Government have yet to agree how the broadcaster will be funded after its current charter expires. The BBC warns that delay could mean further cuts, while ministers say no final decision has been taken.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Time is running out’: Inside the fraught BBC talks to replace licence fee

segments.body: The BBC is seeking a replacement for the £180 licence fee, with ministers expected to publish a White Paper in December. The broadcaster says cancellations and other pressures have left a £500m funding gap and plans to save £500m, including through 2,000 job cuts. Insiders fear the funding timetable could slip into next year.

segments.title: Options and disagreements
segments.body: Director-general Matt Brittin has suggested a lower household levy, but the Treasury is understood to oppose a measure that could be presented as a new tax. Other proposals include a broadband levy or a charge on streaming subscriptions or devices. Government sources say discussions are continuing and no final decision has been made.

The current royal charter expires at the end of next year. The BBC has already announced programme and service cuts, while regional leaders are pressing for the broadcaster to retain plans connected to Birmingham. The eventual settlement may also set requirements for news, education and regional programming.

content.headline: Denmark’s oldest person says she was enrolled in Nazi party during occupation
content.shortHeadline: Denmark’s oldest person confirms Nazi party membership
content.standfirst: Kirsten Schwalbe, 112, confirmed she was enrolled in Denmark’s DNSAP in 1941. Historians caution that the surviving membership register does not establish why someone joined, how long they belonged or whether they were active.

image.caption: Kirsten Schwalbe, who confirmed she was enrolled in Denmark’s Nazi party in 1941.

sources.originalTitle: Danmarks længstlevende var medlem af dansk nazistparti

segments.body: Kirsten Schwalbe, described as the longest-lived person in Denmark’s history, confirmed to TV Midtvest that she was enrolled in the Danish National Socialist Workers’ Party during the German occupation. She said her husband asked her to join and that she was not interested in politics.

segments.title: What the record does—and does not—show
segments.body: Two historians independently confirmed that her name appears in the DNSAP membership register, though her surname is misspelled there. Historian Charlie Krautwald said the register records whether someone enrolled, not why, how long they were a member or whether they were active. The publisher of a recent book about Schwalbe said it had not known about this part of her history and would consider whether changes were needed.

content.headline: Danish party leaders’ defamation dispute ends with Lidegaard acquitted
content.shortHeadline: Lidegaard acquitted in Danish party leaders’ defamation case
content.standfirst: Martin Lidegaard was acquitted after Morten Messerschmidt sued over comments about his immigration proposals. The first court case between Danish party leaders tested the boundaries of political speech.

sources.originalTitle: LIVE Lidegaard frifindes for injurier mod Messerschmidt
Historisk retssag mellem partiledere bliver afgjort i dag

segments.body: A court acquitted Martin Lidegaard of defaming Danish People’s Party leader Morten Messerschmidt, DR reports. Messerschmidt sued over Lidegaard’s description of proposals to deport tens of thousands of people, including if they could not support themselves. The suit sought recognition of defamation, not a penalty or damages.

segments.title: The free-speech question
segments.body: The case was the first lawsuit between Danish party leaders and was heard by a panel of three judges, an unusual arrangement for a civil case. Before the ruling, law professor Sten Schaumburg-Müller said political debate needs broad freedom but that there are limits to false and irrelevant accusations. He considered Messerschmidt’s case difficult to win.

content.headline: Archaeologists uncover more than 1,000 graves in Copenhagen park
content.shortHeadline: More than 1,000 skeletons uncovered in Copenhagen park
content.standfirst: Archaeologists are excavating a 19th-century paupers’ burial ground in Nørrebro before Hans Tavsens Park is redesigned to manage cloudburst water. The remains offer a rare window into the lives of Copenhagen’s poor.

image.caption: Archaeologists excavate the former paupers’ cemetery in Hans Tavsens Park, Copenhagen.

sources.originalTitle: Arkæologer graver over 1.000 skeletter op i København

segments.body: Archaeologists from Copenhagen Museum are excavating more than 1,000 people buried at a 19th-century paupers’ cemetery beneath Hans Tavsens Park in Nørrebro. The remains can help researchers learn about the poor population of the period and the city’s history.

segments.title: A park being reshaped
segments.body: The excavation is taking place ahead of plans to turn the park and Hans Tavsens Gade into a connected green space that can collect cloudburst water and reduce flooding. Most of the skeletons will be stored and studied at the Anthropological Laboratory; some will be reburied in the park. The work is expected to continue into next year.

content.headline: Struer expands calls to older residents after pilot finds health needs
content.shortHeadline: Struer expands wellbeing calls to older residents living alone
content.standfirst: A pilot offering calls to people over 67 who live alone or feel lonely is being extended to more parts of Struer municipality. One resident received advice and equipment to help with her breathing condition.

sources.originalTitle: Margrethe fik et opkald fra kommunen: Hvordan har du det?

segments.body: Struer municipality is expanding a pilot that calls residents over 67 who live alone or feel lonely, after positive results on Thyholm and Jegindø. About 130 people in those areas accepted an offer of a conversation about health and wellbeing.

During a call, health advisers can offer guidance and arrange a follow-up or home visit if needed. Margrethe Tøstesen, who has COPD and breathing difficulties, received a PEP breathing device after speaking to an adviser. The scheme is now being extended to Gimsing and Resen parishes.

content.headline: Study offers clues to why small dogs may live longer than large breeds
content.shortHeadline: Dog blood study finds differences linked to size and ageing
content.standfirst: Researchers analysing blood samples from nearly 900 dogs found cell activity linked to DNA errors was higher in large dogs. The study may help explain earlier cancer risk, but scientists say they do not yet know why the differences occur.

image.caption: A dog in Denmark; researchers are studying how ageing differs between small and large breeds.

sources.originalTitle: Forskere finder mulig forklaring på, hvorfor små hunde lever længere end store

segments.body: Researchers analysed blood samples from nearly 900 dogs and found differences in cell activity associated with ageing. Large dogs showed more activity in areas linked to genetic errors, which may raise the risk of diseases including cancer. The study was published in the journal Science.

segments.title: What researchers still do not know
segments.body: Cancer is the most common cause of death among dogs, and large breeds tend to develop it earlier, researcher Maja Louise Arendt told DR. The study also found a tendency for male dogs to age slightly faster than females. Researchers have not established why either difference occurs.

content.headline: How Fontaines D.C. went from Dublin dive bars to stadium headliners
content.shortHeadline: Fontaines D.C.’s unlikely rise from Dublin dive bars to stadiums
content.standfirst: As the band releases Dopamine Chamber, fans and collaborators trace a rise built on songwriting, touring and radio support—not a manufactured viral moment. Their success, one supporter argues, is the mainstream coming to them.

image.caption: Fontaines D.C., with frontman Grian Chatten at the centre.

sources.originalTitle: ‘The mainstream has come to them’: how did Fontaines DC go from Dublin dive bars to headlining stadiums?

segments.body: Fontaines D.C. formed at Dublin’s BIMM Music Institute in 2014 and built their audience through relentless gigging, increasingly ambitious records and early champions including BBC Radio 6 Music’s Steve Lamacq. Their first album, Dogrel, reached the UK and Irish top 10 in 2019; their latest, Dopamine Chamber, arrives as they prepare for major festival slots and stadium dates.

segments.title: A route beyond the algorithm
segments.body: The band’s rise has not followed the usual viral playbook. Marketing consultant Liam Ward describes their relatively restrained social-media presence and says the fans’ online activity looks organic. Kneecap’s Mo Chara points to their music and politics, including a homelessness benefit and opposition to the genocide in Palestine, as part of their appeal. The article suggests that talent, work, support and luck all played a part.

perspectives.body: Kneecap’s Mo Chara sums up the band’s relationship with commercial success this way: “The mainstream has come to them rather than the other way round.”

content.headline: Shygirl on the work, risks and love behind her new rock-leaning album
content.shortHeadline: Shygirl turns to rock—and makes success on her own terms
content.standfirst: The London artist’s forthcoming album Swallow! takes her from club sounds towards soaring guitars, with intimacy and vulnerability at its centre. She reflects on a working-class upbringing, ambition and the limits women face in music.

image.caption: Shygirl in 2026.

sources.originalTitle: ‘I need to prove my family’s sacrifice was worth it’: how pop auteur Shygirl slogged her way to the top

segments.body: Shygirl says Swallow!, her second album, is an expansive rock record inspired in part by the security and vulnerability of her relationship. Its guitars and crashing drums mark a change from the hyperpop, UK garage and electronic sounds of her earlier work. She also co-directed a series of connected videos, shaped as an elliptical thriller.

segments.title: A career built through persistence
segments.body: Born Blane Muise, Shygirl grew up in south-east London, where her parents worked a range of jobs. She says their sacrifices helped drive her to make a better life through music, though success has brought “mad guilt” as well as new opportunities. She describes women as facing a persistent barrier in the industry and says she wants to work with people who welcome difference.

content.headline: Richard Thompson on songcraft, folk history and a life on stage
content.shortHeadline: Richard Thompson on folk, fiction and the strange life of touring
content.standfirst: The 77-year-old guitarist answers questions about his new album, his songwriting and the musicians around him. His memories range from Sandy Denny’s anxious car rides to a knife-wielding audience member who wanted “something normal”.

image.caption: Richard Thompson.

sources.originalTitle: ‘A guy held a knife to my throat and said: play something normal!’ Richard Thompson on crazy crowds, his beloved beret and Sandy Denny’s driving skills

segments.body: Richard Thompson says the characters in his songs are not necessarily portraits of himself or people he knows. “Beeswing,” often associated with folk singer Anne Briggs, also draws on stories told by a man who visited Thompson’s Suffolk home for odd jobs, as well as Sandy Denny’s sense of Briggs as a free spirit. “I need credit as a writer of fiction, too,” he says.

segments.title: On the road
segments.body: Thompson recalls touring with Denny, jamming with John Martyn and turning down approaches from the Eagles, the Animals and the Band. One Swedish performance in the 1970s stands out: an audience member held a knife to his throat and demanded that he play “something normal”. Thompson says he wondered what “normal” meant, and may have played a Buddy Holly cover.

content.headline: Weird Baile pushes Brazilian funk into grime and drill territory
content.shortHeadline: Weird Baile takes Brazilian funk to its outer limits
content.standfirst: Collected Rips 2004-2024 brings together two decades of work by four producers who strip baile funk to bass, vocals and rhythm. The result draws on British grime and drill without simply copying either scene.

image.caption: Weird Baile, whose compilation brings together productions from 2004 to 2024.

sources.originalTitle: Weird Baile: Collected Rips 2004-2024 review – a hallucinatory trip to baile funk’s outer limits

segments.body: Weird Baile began releasing its own tracks in 2017, after producers JLZ, VHOOR, Mu540 and DJ RaMeMes connected through baile funk edits on SoundCloud. Their new compilation gathers two decades of lo-fi productions, tracing a sound that pares back the Brazilian genre’s elements and brings them into contact with British dance music.

segments.title: A productive collision
segments.body: The review hears the collection at its most distinctive when it disrupts its influences: “Grime Do Weird Baile” turns the force of a Skepta and JME beat into a bouncing dance-floor track, while other pieces lean towards drill bass or dubstep. Its abrasive, deliberately sparse production makes the compilation feel both recognisable and unsettled.

content.headline: Rachel Chinouriri finds her sweet spot in pop’s messy emotions
content.shortHeadline: Rachel Chinouriri makes room for messy feelings on her second album
content.standfirst: On i think i spoke too soon, the London singer pairs brighter, more polished production with conversational songs about love, insecurity and public embarrassment. Pitchfork finds that her emotional instincts keep the album grounded.

sources.originalTitle: I think I spoke too soon

segments.body: Rachel Chinouriri’s second album keeps the alt-rock and radio-pop influences of her 2024 debut, but gives them a shinier, more synthesised finish. Pitchfork finds that the polished sound occasionally obscures her voice, especially early on, before the record settles into sharper, more individual songs.

segments.title: Humour with a pulse
segments.body: The review highlights the rom-com-like middle stretch, where arcade sounds, guitars and violin frame Chinouriri’s anxious crush songs. Tracks such as “I’m a star” and “AAAHHH!!!” let her be funny and melodramatic without losing sight of genuine insecurity. What distinguishes her, Pitchfork argues, is the emotional precision beneath the relatable-pop persona.

perspectives.body: Pitchfork’s central reservation is that the album’s smooth production can sometimes flatten Chinouriri’s vocals; it argues that the record is strongest once her distinctive, playful delivery comes forward.

content.headline: Jon Hassell’s final Pentimento album captures his unmistakable musical voice
content.shortHeadline: Jon Hassell’s final Pentimento album returns to his singular sound
content.standfirst: Built chiefly from the trumpeter’s last live performance, Music Is Invisible reshapes old and new material into a collage of tension, echo and electronic texture. The review hears a distinctive presence still anchoring the music.

sources.originalTitle: Music Is Invisible (Pentimento Volume Three)

segments.body: Music Is Invisible completes Jon Hassell’s Pentimento series, assembled by Jeff Rona from live, studio and archival recordings. Its main source is Hassell’s final London performance, in 2015, with multi-instrumentalists Rick Cox and John von Seggern. Hassell later encouraged Rona to use the recording as a foundation for new pieces; Hassell died in 2021.

segments.title: A presence in the sound
segments.body: The review describes the album’s mood as quietly tense, with Hassell’s processed trumpet remaining its centre of gravity. On “Club Gris-Gris”, the horn moves against dub-like echoes; the long closing track, “Electric Forest”, builds from talking drums, fraying trumpet and scattered electronic detail before returning to earlier material.

content.headline: SUPREME MAGNETIC 3 deepens Harlem rapper Errol Holden’s vivid portraits
content.shortHeadline: Errol Holden’s SUPREME MAGNETIC 3 digs deeper into Harlem memories
content.standfirst: The prolific rapper turns street-level memories into dense, fast-moving vignettes over shadowy production. Pitchfork calls the album an absorbing extension of a singular storytelling voice.

sources.originalTitle: SUPREME MAGNETIC 3

segments.body: Errol Holden’s third Supreme Magnetic release continues the Harlem rapper’s autobiographical writing, built from details about neighbourhoods, people and the past. On the 33-minute album, his rapid, technically dense verses sit within spacious, ominous beats, most of them produced by the returning 2000 Souls.

The review praises Holden’s ability to make fragments feel vivid and connected, from references to old New York and childhood encounters with the Five Percenters to cast-iron pans and 1990s Reeboks. It sees the album’s restless accumulation of images—not conventional song structure—as the strength of his storytelling.

content.headline: Cameron Winter’s Carnegie Hall set turns new songs into living standards
content.shortHeadline: Cameron Winter’s Carnegie Hall performance makes new songs feel lived
content.standfirst: The Geese frontman’s solo live album documents a concert that was both a musical showcase and a moment of public mythmaking. Pitchfork singles out the new material and Winter’s exposed, expressive piano playing.

sources.originalTitle: Live at Carnegie Hall

segments.body: Live at Carnegie Hall records Cameron Winter’s 11 December 2025 performance, released alongside Paul Thomas Anderson’s concert film. Winter, then 24, plays piano and guitar, including three previously unreleased songs. Pitchfork hears an intimate set that gives his music room to breathe, with the piano revealing a side of his musicianship less prominent in Geese.

segments.title: A performance taking shape
segments.body: The review notes that Winter sounds nervous at the beginning, then grows more assured as the concert unfolds. It praises the new songs, especially “If You Turn Back Now”, and argues that the live arrangements transform material from his solo debut into something larger and less tethered to the difficult circumstances of its creation.

content.headline: NAZA and the difficult questions of putting perpetrators on screen
content.shortHeadline: NAZA raises hard questions about films that give perpetrators a voice
content.standfirst: The documentary’s interviews with Israeli military insiders have provoked debate over whose testimony is heard and what it can reveal. A wider look at perpetrator cinema weighs its value against the risks of centring those responsible for atrocities.

image.caption: NAZA features anonymised Israeli intelligence personnel discussing the assault on Gaza.

sources.originalTitle: Calling the shots: what NAZA says about perpetrator cinema
NAZA review – Israeli intelligence officers cast chilling light on civilian deaths
Jonathan Glazer says Israel’s retaliation over NAZA ‘more venal’ than anticipated

segments.body: NAZA, directed by Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, features anonymised Israeli intelligence personnel discussing their role in the assault on Gaza. The Guardian’s analysis places it in the tradition of “perpetrator cinema”, alongside The Act of Killing and Standard Operating Procedure, and asks what these films can show about the people and systems behind atrocities.

perspectives.body: The Guardian’s review argues that anonymity weakens NAZA’s testimony: the interviewees’ accounts are chilling, it says, but the film’s impact is diminished when no one can be persuaded to attach a name and face to them.

segments.title: The argument over access and responsibility
segments.body: The analysis notes criticism that NAZA gives perpetrators a platform while Palestinian accounts of Gaza have already been extensively documented. It also describes the Israeli government’s threats against the filmmakers and its attempt to counter the documentary with a project of its own. Jonathan Glazer, the film’s executive producer, said the response was “much more venal” than he expected.

segments.title: What the films can—and cannot—do
segments.body: These works offer no easy catharsis, the Guardian argues. Their value lies in probing how ordinary institutions and people become implicated in violence, and in making viewers confront what they would rather reject. NAZA’s interviewees describe systems used to target Hamas operatives while anticipating civilian deaths; those claims are presented by the film and its reporting, not as independently established findings in the supplied coverage.

content.headline: Fjord turns a family dispute into a debate about Norway and Romania
content.shortHeadline: Fjord’s family drama exposes a live debate in Norway and Romania
content.standfirst: Cristian Mungiu’s Cannes-winning film echoes a real child-welfare case and has divided audiences over religion, discipline and the state’s role. Its reception reveals how sharply law, public belief and personal experience can diverge.

image.caption: A scene from Cristian Mungiu’s film Fjord.

sources.originalTitle: Dogmatic Nordic liberals v eastern family values: culture-clash drama Fjord touches nerves in Norway and Romania

segments.body: Fjord echoes the 2015 case of a Romanian Pentecostal couple in Norway whose five children were removed by child-welfare authorities amid concerns about corporal punishment and religious indoctrination. The children were later returned. In Romania, Mungiu’s fictionalised film drew a large one-night audience and reopened a charged debate about the case.

segments.title: A disagreement over what the film says
segments.body: Some viewers read Fjord as a critique of dogmatic liberalism; others say it softens a moral line on corporal punishment and gives the family undue sympathy. The article stresses that Norway and Romania both prohibit corporal punishment, while beliefs and practice differ, and notes that European human-rights rulings prompted changes to Norway’s child-welfare procedures.

perspectives.body: The article’s writer reads Fjord as a warning about institutions and communities convinced of their own good intentions: any system, the writer argues, must be able to imagine that it may be wrong.

content.headline: The Face of Horror is Anna Biller’s playful tribute to Hammer films
content.shortHeadline: Anna Biller’s The Face of Horror revives Hammer-style melodrama
content.standfirst: The director of The Love Witch turns to garish colour, Gothic revenge and deadpan humour for a film inspired by a Japanese ghost story and British 1960s horror. The Guardian review finds a future cult midnight movie.

image.caption: Jonah Hauer-King and Kristine Froseth in The Face of Horror.

sources.originalTitle: The Face of Horror review – a future cult classic delights with playful spin on Hammer horror

segments.body: Anna Biller’s The Face of Horror builds a cod-medieval tale around Yotsuya Kaidan, the Japanese ghost story that has also inspired filmmakers including Takashi Miike and Hideo Nakata. Its look and tone evoke the vivid, melodramatic horror films made by Britain’s Hammer Films in the 1960s.

Jonah Hauer-King plays Edward, a knight who murders the family members opposing his marriage to Eleanor, played by Kristine Froseth. As Edward turns towards another noblewoman, supernatural revenge gathers. The review praises the film’s sustained, deadpan excess, particularly a courtly Danse Macabre scene, and predicts a future for it as a cult midnight movie.

content.headline: The adaptation does not have to be faithful to make a great film
content.shortHeadline: Why the best film adaptations often leave the book behind
content.standfirst: From The Shining to Children of Men, Louise Willder argues that adaptation is a translation between forms, not a test of fidelity. The filmmaker’s own vision may matter more than whether readers recognise their imagined version.

image.caption: A selection of films discussed in an essay on adapting books for the screen.

sources.originalTitle: An open book: how to make a great film adaptation, from The Shining to Trainspotting

segments.body: Louise Willder’s argument is that neither the quality of the source nor strict loyalty to it determines whether an adaptation works. Jaws and The Godfather became screen classics; Trainspotting and The Leopard show that celebrated novels can, too. A film must find its own visual language rather than simply reproduce a book’s events.

segments.title: Taking liberties
segments.body: Willder points to Children of Men, which turns P.D. James’s novel into a dystopian thriller, and to Sally Potter’s Orlando, which reimagines Virginia Woolf’s book. She argues that reverence can make a film feel hollow, while casting and performance can make unexpected choices work. Adaptation, in the end, is also a matter of the feelings and sensations a film leaves behind.

content.headline: You Can See Everything keeps Elizabeth Holmes’ story unresolved
content.shortHeadline: Elizabeth Holmes remains an enigma in You Can See Everything
content.standfirst: Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim follow the convicted Theranos founder before she enters prison, letting her insist that she did nothing wrong. The film turns that uneasy access into a broader question about truth and image-making.

sources.originalTitle: 'As famous and defiant as ever': Why Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes remains the US's most fascinating fraudster

segments.body: You Can See Everything follows Elizabeth Holmes, her partner and their children in the weeks before she reported to prison in 2023. Holmes, convicted of defrauding investors, maintains in conversations with Nathan Fielder that her blood-testing device worked and that she did not lie. The film offers no settled answer about whether she believes her own account.

segments.title: Access without a verdict
segments.body: BBC Culture describes the film as a comic but unsettling hall of mirrors: Fielder’s visibly sceptical reactions undercut Holmes’s claims, while another person introduced later challenges both her account and Fielder’s own position. The directors leave the central question open, turning the film into an examination of how documentary access can shape—and complicate—a public image.

content.headline: La Bola Negra links three gay lives across a century of Spanish history
content.shortHeadline: La Bola Negra traces gay desire and memory across Spanish history
content.standfirst: Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi’s film connects three men’s stories across 1932, 1937 and 2017. Its ambitious form, performances and visual style have made it a major contender in early awards conversation.

sources.originalTitle: 'Immediately spellbinding': Four reasons why gay Spanish epic La Bola Negra could win the Oscar for best picture

segments.body: La Bola Negra follows Sebastian, a conscript in Franco’s army; Carlos, a young man shut out of an exclusive club amid rumours about his sexuality; and Alberto, a historian in 2017 investigating an unexpected family inheritance. The film draws on the work of poet and playwright Federico García Lorca and connects its timelines through memory, art and repression.

segments.title: A film gaining attention
segments.body: The film won the People’s Choice Award at the Toronto Film Festival after a Cannes reception that prompted a distributor bidding war. BBC Culture notes its awards momentum and praises the ensemble, including first-time actor Álvaro Lafuente Calvo and Penélope Cruz. The article presents a best-picture nomination as a possibility, not a settled outcome.

content.headline: Klara and the Sun turns Kazuo Ishiguro’s AI fable into a sentimental film
content.shortHeadline: Klara and the Sun is a misjudged, sentimental AI fable
content.standfirst: Taika Waititi adapts Kazuo Ishiguro’s story of an artificial friend into a tale of love and grief. The Guardian review argues that the film’s whimsical tone weakens its ideas about artificial intelligence.

image.caption: Jenna Ortega as Klara in Klara and the Sun.

sources.originalTitle: Klara and the Sun review – Taika Waititi’s manic pixie dream robot sci-fi is a sentimental mess

segments.body: In Taika Waititi’s adaptation, Jenna Ortega plays Klara, a solar-powered artificial friend bought for Josie, a lonely teenager with an unspecified illness. The film follows Klara as she tries to understand the family and the world around her, including her belief that the sun may help Josie.

The Guardian’s review finds the film’s humour mannered and its emotional turns unearned, arguing that it says little about AI, love or grief. It contrasts the result with more persuasive screen treatments of artificial intelligence, while acknowledging that the underlying question of whether a robot can have real feelings remains difficult to dramatise.

perspectives.body: The Guardian critic’s verdict is sharply negative: Waititi’s film is described as a sentimental, laborious mess, with its whimsical tone blunting the ideas it might have explored.

content.headline: Last One Laughing adds a no-screaming rule for its Halloween special
content.shortHeadline: Last One Laughing’s Halloween special bans screams as well as laughs
content.standfirst: The comedians must keep a straight face—and now avoid shrieking—as the hit show leans into horror for a special. Its contestants and host explain why surprise, strategy and the pressure of being watched make the format work.

image.caption: Daisy May Cooper in Last One Laughing: Halloween.

sources.originalTitle: ‘I didn’t know I was a screamer. Turns out I am’ – the spooky secrets of Last One Laughing: Halloween

segments.body: The Halloween special of Last One Laughing adds a new rule: contestants must not scream as well as refrain from laughing. Phil Wang says he had not realised he was a screamer until filming. The lineup includes Lou Sanders, Tom Allen, Reece Shearsmith, Daisy May Cooper and Harriet Dyer, with Jimmy Carr returning as host.

segments.title: Comedy as competition
segments.body: Carr says laughs and screams draw on the same instinct for surprise, while Wang describes the show as a mix of gameshow and psychological experiment. The comics talk about tactics, the strain of staying composed and the production’s close attention to every reaction. The article says the first series became Prime Video’s biggest UK launch at the time and later won a Bafta for Best Entertainment Programme.

content.headline: Esther Rantzen’s kindness and campaigning live on in readers’ memories
content.shortHeadline: Readers remember Esther Rantzen’s generosity and public service
content.standfirst: Guardian readers recall the late presenter’s warmth, curiosity and commitment to people who might otherwise go unheard. Their memories range from a formative television programme to her work with Childline and bereaved families.

image.caption: Esther Rantzen, a familiar figure on British television.

sources.originalTitle: ‘She asked me to lie on her feet while she did sit-ups’: your memories of Esther Rantzen

segments.body: Readers remember Esther Rantzen welcoming them into television production, encouraging a future midwife after a programme about bereavement, and bringing her energy to social-work and Childline events. Several describe her personal attention to people around her, as well as her determination to spotlight children, families and volunteers.

segments.title: A legacy in personal encounters
segments.body: The recollections also record the reach of Rantzen’s broadcasting: one reader recalls The Big Time visiting their family home, while another remembers the investigative and comic blend of That’s Life!. Together, the accounts present her legacy through both public campaigns and small acts of encouragement.

content.headline: Seven new shows to stream, from The Audacity to Nobody Wants This
content.shortHeadline: This week’s streaming picks include The Audacity and Nobody Wants This
content.standfirst: The Guardian’s guide ranges from a satire of Silicon Valley to a Halloween comedy special and a documentary about online grooming. It offers a quick route through the week’s notable new television.

image.caption: Billy Magnussen and Sarah Goldberg in The Audacity.

sources.originalTitle: The Audacity to Nobody Wants This: the seven best shows to stream this week

segments.body: The guide’s leading pick is The Audacity, Jonathan Glatzer’s comedy about tech executives and the money, therapy and dubious business practices surrounding them. The article says it aims for a Succession-like blend of comedy and horror, though it does not reach that show’s heights.

segments.title: Other choices this week
segments.body: The selection also includes a four-part Last One Laughing Halloween special, a two-part documentary about the grooming and murder of teenager Breck Bednar, a new Lupin series and a crime documentary about European police access to the encrypted Sky ECC app. The guide additionally points to the latest Nobody Wants This and a comic story about killer garden gnomes.

content.headline: Time turns a young offenders’ prison into a study of masculinity
content.shortHeadline: Time explores anger, love and masculinity in a young offenders’ prison
content.standfirst: Jimmy McGovern’s third series follows boys in a young offenders’ institution and the guards who control them. The review links their violence to isolation, damaged relationships and a prison system stripped of rehabilitation.

image.caption: David Tennant as prison officer Bobby Bailey in Time.

sources.originalTitle: Time picks up where Adolescence left off

segments.body: The third series of Time is set in a young offenders’ institution, where boys serving sentences for serious violence live under strict confinement. The review follows prisoners including Ushindi, Peter and James, alongside prison officer Bobby, as authority and aggression shape daily life behind the gates.

segments.title: Anger in a system of isolation
segments.body: The article argues that the show connects violence to an inability to express vulnerability and to seek love. It also points to the institution’s limited provision for rehabilitation: Bobby recalls a time when prisoners had libraries, training and education, contrasted with a present in which they can be locked in their cells for most of the day. The review says the drama offers no simple fix, but shows what unchecked anger can cost.

content.headline: Sarah Solemani brings class, grief and ambition to The Party
content.shortHeadline: Sarah Solemani on class, grief and making The Party
content.standfirst: The actor, writer and showrunner leads a new drama about a working-class journalist among wealthy political circles. She discusses adapting Elizabeth Day’s novel, losing her mother as a teenager and the changes she has seen in Hollywood.

image.caption: Sarah Solemani, actor, writer and showrunner.

sources.originalTitle: Sarah Solemani: ‘I performed at my mum’s hospice bed two weeks before she died’

segments.body: The Party centres on Martin, a working-class journalist played by Luke Evans, and Ben, a Tory politician played by Tom Cullen, whose friendship has a dark secret. Sarah Solemani plays Martin’s pregnant wife, Lucy, and also wrote and showran the series, adapted from Elizabeth Day’s 2017 novel.

segments.title: Writing from experience
segments.body: Solemani says she has long wanted to write about the British class system and used her research to shape the show’s political world. She also recalls performing two monologues at her mother’s hospice bed at 16, shortly before her mother died. She says the experience of grief helped drive her towards a life in theatre and television.

content.headline: Ellie Taylor on taking Strictly’s It Takes Two in a new direction
content.shortHeadline: Ellie Taylor wants It Takes Two to embrace Strictly’s silliness
content.standfirst: The comedian and presenter says she wants the spin-off to join the wider Strictly conversation while keeping its playful spirit. She also reflects on audience criticism, social anxiety and the job she hoped to land.

image.caption: Ellie Taylor, the new host of Strictly Come Dancing: It Takes Two.

sources.originalTitle: Ellie Taylor on the Strictly backlash: ‘People don’t like change’

segments.body: Ellie Taylor has taken over as host of Strictly Come Dancing: It Takes Two. A former Strictly contestant, she says she wants the programme to engage with fan conversation and lean into the show’s camp, ridiculous side. Early criticism over a panel without professional dancers was answered with a panel of pros the following day.

segments.title: Learning to live with change
segments.body: Taylor auditioned for the main Saturday-night presenting role but says she is happy with It Takes Two. Asked about criticism of Strictly’s new hosts, she argues that viewers can be resistant to change and says the dancing remains central. She describes herself as an introvert who experiences social anxiety despite her frequent on-screen work.

content.headline: Doctor Who’s uncertain future leaves fans waiting for a return
content.shortHeadline: Doctor Who faces an uncertain pause after its latest revival
content.standfirst: The BBC has ended its Disney+ partnership and cancelled a planned Christmas special, leaving the long-running series without a current Doctor. Fans and television voices disagree about what went wrong, but want the show back on screen.

image.caption: Several actors who have played the Doctor, including Ncuti Gatwa and Jodie Whittaker.

sources.originalTitle: The sad, slow death of Doctor Who

segments.body: After Ncuti Gatwa’s departure, the BBC has cancelled a planned Doctor Who Christmas special and ended its collaboration with Disney+. The corporation says it is seeking a new production partner through a competitive tender, but none has yet been announced. The series currently has no Doctor in place.

segments.title: What should come next?
segments.body: Fans and contributors point to several possible causes, from confusing scripts and audience decline to the expectations attached to the Disney+ deal. Comedian Frank Skinner says the show did not need a huge investment to tell a good story and worries about how long it has been kept off air. The article argues that its future should preserve the series’ capacity to change while respecting its core identity.

perspectives.body: Lifelong fan Frank Skinner’s plea is direct: the programme should be back on screen, and whoever takes it on should avoid tampering too much with its origin story.

content.headline: Tonight on TV: Quentin Tarantino returns to Graham Norton’s sofa
content.shortHeadline: Tonight’s TV guide: Tarantino, zombies and a family heist
content.standfirst: The evening listings include Quentin Tarantino discussing his new West End play, a zombie raid on the Empire State Building and a crime comedy starring Stanley Tucci. The guide also points to a film about Kate Moss sitting for Lucian Freud.

image.caption: Quentin Tarantino, appearing on The Graham Norton Show.

sources.originalTitle: TV tonight: Quentin Tarantino makes a rare appearance on Graham Norton’s sofa

segments.body: The guide’s headline pick is Tarantino’s return to The Graham Norton Show, where he is due to discuss The Popinjay Cavalier, his West End farce starring Sacha Baron Cohen. Ellen DeGeneres, Colin Farrell and Gemma Chan are also listed as guests, with Suede providing the music.

segments.title: More viewing choices
segments.body: Other recommendations include The Walking Dead: Dead City, in which Maggie and Negan recruit a team for a dangerous mission in New York, and Masterplan, a heist comedy starring Stanley Tucci. The guide also highlights Moss & Freud, about supermodel Kate Moss sitting for painter Lucian Freud.

content.headline: Penguin Colony turns an Antarctic odyssey into a strange, searching game
content.shortHeadline: Penguin Colony is an unsettling Antarctic adventure with ideas to unsp
content.standfirst: This exploration game sends a penguin through an Antarctic landscape of Nazis, Lovecraftian horrors and fragments of human language. The Guardian finds its uneven mechanics outweighed by an ambitious, unsettling whole.

image.caption: A penguin explores the Antarctic world of Penguin Colony.

sources.originalTitle: Penguin Colony review – an Antarctic odyssey of Nazis and Lovecraftian horrors

segments.body: In Penguin Colony, players guide a penguin across Antarctica, following an expedition in search of an uncanny entity. The game draws on H.P. Lovecraft’s At the Mountains of Madness, but recasts the journey through a bird’s-eye view of the expedition’s human hubris, with Nazis and other horrors occupying the landscape.

segments.title: Learning to look around
segments.body: The world moves from fishing huts and snowfields to stone labyrinths, alien obelisks and crevasses. Players can switch between penguins with different abilities, while collecting words rather than conventional treasure. The review acknowledges occasional audio and control problems, but praises the game’s finale for challenging Lovecraft’s racism and Nazi barbarism and inviting a less human-centred view of the world.

content.headline: Ocarina of Time’s Switch 2 remake tests what a classic should look like
content.shortHeadline: Ocarina of Time’s remake updates Hyrule without losing its shape
content.standfirst: Nintendo’s Switch 2 version adds modern controls, 4K detail and a newly orchestrated soundtrack to its 1998 landmark. The preview weighs those improvements against the risks of revising a beloved visual style.

image.caption: Link in the Nintendo Switch 2 remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time.

sources.originalTitle: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time preview – Link faces his scariest challenge yet: the 4K era

segments.body: The Switch 2 remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time brings changes to movement, camera control and menus, alongside updated visuals and an orchestrated soundtrack. The Guardian’s hands-on preview says Link feels significantly different to control, while familiar dungeons retain the appeal of structured puzzles and exploration.

segments.title: A new look for a familiar world
segments.body: The preview questions whether the more detailed 4K presentation risks mistaking surface polish for artistic purpose, especially in Link’s glassy-eyed design. It also considers an alternative reading: former Zelda art director Takaya Imamura suggested the character’s appearance may reflect Japanese puppet theatre. The piece notes that the visual effect feels coherent in motion, even if Nintendo’s intent remains unknown.

content.headline: Could independent arcades bring gaming back to the high street?
content.shortHeadline: A new wave of independent arcades could revive social gaming
content.standfirst: After years of sprawling games designed to keep players online, some developers are returning to shorter, focused experiences. New independent venues may offer a social alternative to playing at home.

image.caption: A video game arcade attracting a new audience.

sources.originalTitle: Ready player one? Why the games arcade is having a rebirth

segments.body: The Guardian’s games writer sees a shift away from “forever games” towards focused experiences shaped by arcade conventions. They point to games such as Star Wars Galactic Racer and Ace Combat 8, which offer a defined play experience rather than asking players to build their lives around a persistent online world.

segments.title: A place to play together
segments.body: The article argues for arcades that curate new and classic games and build local communities, rather than simply placing old coin-ops in a bar. Games journalist Will Freeman points to smaller ventures, including London’s forthcoming NQ Japan and Pixel Bunker in Milton Keynes, as examples of a quieter shift towards expert-led venues. The hope is that arcades can restore some of gaming’s social life to high streets.

content.headline: A £350 GTA collector’s box reflects gaming’s growing price divide
content.shortHeadline: What a £350 GTA collector’s box says about gaming’s rising cost
content.standfirst: Rockstar’s merchandise set for Grand Theft Auto 6 does not include the game itself. The Guardian argues that its price reflects a wider divide between mobile players and those able to pay more for console gaming and collectibles.

image.caption: The Grand Theft Auto VI: The Goodtime State – Vice City Collection merchandise box.

sources.originalTitle: What the £350 Grand Theft Auto ‘collector’s box’ says about the escalating cost of gaming

segments.body: Rockstar has announced a £350 Grand Theft Auto 6 collector’s box of merchandise, but it does not include the game or a download code. The game itself is listed at £70, making the full outlay £420 for buyers who want both. The writer, a collector of gaming memorabilia, says the price is unusually high even by special-edition standards.

segments.title: A growing divide
segments.body: The article connects the box to wider console and game price rises, arguing that high-end gaming is increasingly a luxury purchase. It cites an estimate that about 80% of players use free or low-cost mobile games, while the remaining 20% account for a disproportionate share of spending on console and PC games. The writer worries that the games they value are becoming harder to access and own physically.

content.headline: Leap hours will replace leap seconds to reduce risks to computer systems
content.shortHeadline: Leap hours to replace leap seconds and ease risks to computer systems
content.standfirst: International timekeepers have voted to let atomic and astronomical time drift further apart before making a correction. The first leap hour is not expected for thousands of years, but the change is intended to avoid disruptive one-second adjustments.

image.caption: A clock at the Royal Observatory, Greenwich, through which the prime meridian passes.

sources.originalTitle: How an accelerating Earth led experts to adopt the leap hour
Time is a-changin’: say goodbye to the leap second

segments.body: Delegates from 69 countries have voted to replace leap seconds with leap hours. From next year, coordinated universal time can drift by as much as an hour from astronomical time before a correction is needed—a threshold the sources say is unlikely to be reached for thousands of years. The aim is to reduce the risk of computer and infrastructure failures caused by minutes with 61 or 59 seconds.

perspectives.body: The Verge reports that the change was brought forward from a 2035 target to May 2027, after concern that the Earth’s changing rotation might require the first negative leap second—a correction never attempted before.

segments.title: Why the adjustment matters
segments.body: Atomic clocks underpin communications, navigation, trading systems and electricity grids, while Earth’s rotation varies. Since 1972, timekeepers have added 27 leap seconds to keep the systems aligned. The Guardian reports that some servers froze or went offline after the 2012 adjustment; officials said testing every interconnected system for a negative leap second would be costly and difficult.

content.headline: Listening to unfamiliar sounds may help people learn a new language
content.shortHeadline: A sharp ear for sound may help with language learning
content.standfirst: A study of Japanese learners of English linked stronger auditory precision with faster, more accurate pronunciation. The researchers say the findings point to listening skills as a potential focus for language teaching, though they do not establish a single best method.

image.caption: A person learning a language by listening to its sounds.

sources.originalTitle: Stop making sense: focus on sounds to help learn a language, study suggests

segments.body: Researchers at UCL and Tohoku University studied 67 Japanese learners of English. Those better able to detect subtle differences in pitch, length and tone in non-speech sounds learned unfamiliar English vowel sounds faster and more accurately. Their brain activity also relied less on a language-processing network associated with applying familiar pronunciation patterns.

The study’s lead author, UCL professor Kazuya Saito-van Poeteren, said the findings challenge the idea that some nationalities are inherently poor at languages. He argued that teaching should develop learners’ ability to hear new sounds, alongside grammar and vocabulary. Lancaster University’s Padraic Monaghan said the study underlines the importance of listening, while noting that learners vary in sound sensitivity.

content.headline: An early flu season does not necessarily mean a worse one, experts say
content.shortHeadline: Early flu season does not necessarily mean a worse one
content.standfirst: Flu activity is rising in the UK earlier than usual, but scientists say timing alone cannot predict the season’s severity. The mix of circulating strains, immunity and other factors will help determine what happens next.

image.caption: Winter respiratory viruses are circulating in the UK earlier than usual.

sources.originalTitle: Why so many people are sick right now

segments.body: UK flu activity is rising earlier than usual, although infection rates were still relatively low when The i Paper reported the trend. The usual peak is in December or January, but it can fall anywhere from October to March. An early start does not by itself mean a more severe season: flu also began early last year, which ended with fewer deaths than average.

segments.title: What may affect the season
segments.body: Experts point to several possible influences, including changes in circulating strains, weather and patterns of social mixing. The strains prevalent during the Southern Hemisphere’s winter can offer clues about what may arrive in the UK months later. The UK Health Security Agency is monitoring the early rise and urging people eligible for a flu vaccine to take it up; the scale and severity of this season remain uncertain.

content.headline: A longevity researcher challenges popular anti-ageing claims
content.shortHeadline: A longevity researcher questions popular anti-ageing claims
content.standfirst: Oxford demographer Saul Newman argues that some headline-grabbing claims about extreme lifespans, “Blue Zones” and anti-ageing treatments rest on weak evidence. The piece also reports challenges to his critique, underscoring how contested parts of the field remain.

image.caption: Oxford demographer Saul Newman, who has written a book critiquing modern longevity research.

sources.originalTitle: I’m a longevity expert. These four anti-ageing myths are junk science

segments.body: Oxford demographer Saul Newman argues that claims about exceptionally long-lived populations can be undermined by unreliable age records, and questions whether so-called Blue Zones have robust evidence for unusually long lifespans. He also criticises telomere-based promises and young-blood transfusions, noting that the latter have no proven clinical benefit for preventing ageing, according to the US Food and Drug Administration.

segments.title: Claims and counterclaims
segments.body: Newman’s account is a critique of longevity research, not a settled verdict on every line of study. The article includes responses: a Sharecare spokesperson said its Blue Zones programmes are scientifically validated, while a spokesperson for Dan Buettner said Newman’s work had been disproven by independent researchers. The evidence and commercial claims should therefore be distinguished from established ways to extend lifespan.

content.headline: Man accused in London hospitals ransomware attack arrested in Germany
content.shortHeadline: Suspect in London hospitals ransomware attack arrested in Germany
content.standfirst: German police have detained a Russian man accused of belonging to the Qilin cybercrime group, which attacked blood-testing provider Synnovis in 2024. The BBC says German investigators are now examining that hack; the suspect has not been convicted.

image.caption: The man accused of involvement in the Qilin cybercrime group was detained in Frankfurt.

sources.originalTitle: Russian man linked to deadly London hospitals hack arrested

segments.body: The 28-year-old, identified by German media as Vladimir K., is accused of being a core member of Qilin, a ransomware group alleged to have hacked thousands of organisations. German police are investigating the 2024 attack on Synnovis, which disrupted pathology services at London hospitals, cancelled operations and affected more than 10,000 appointments.

segments.title: The impact of the Synnovis attack
segments.body: King’s College Hospital NHS Foundation Trust said a patient died unexpectedly after the attack, with a long wait for a blood-test result among several contributing factors identified in its investigation. The BBC reports that British police are also examining whether their inquiry could lead to an unlawful-killing case. The suspect is accused; no finding of guilt is reported.

content.headline: Police and child-safety groups warn online grooming is reaching younger children
content.shortHeadline: Police warn online grooming can reach children as young as five
content.standfirst: Police and child-safety organisations say grooming is taking place across social media, messaging and gaming platforms. Their advice is to keep communication open and make clear that children will not be blamed if they seek help.

image.caption: Police warn that children can be targeted for grooming on social media and gaming sites.

sources.originalTitle: Snapchat and Instagram grooming becoming 'easier'

segments.body: Avon and Somerset Police’s child exploitation prevention officer says children as young as five can be targeted through social media, gaming and messaging services. The NSPCC says Snapchat was mentioned in 324 counselling sessions about online sexual abuse in the year to March 2026, with TikTok and Instagram also frequently named. These figures describe counselling contacts, not the prevalence of abuse across all users.

segments.title: How adults can respond
segments.body: Police and NSPCC staff urge parents to talk with children early, listen without judgement and avoid taking away devices in a way that could make a child feel at fault. The NSPCC says children may be afraid or embarrassed to disclose abuse. A government spokesperson says legislation is being prepared to block children from taking, sharing or viewing nude images on their devices; the report also records disagreement over whether an under-16 social-media ban would be sufficient.

content.headline: England and Wales to criminalise possession of some extreme pornography
content.shortHeadline: New rules will criminalise some extreme pornography from 6 November
content.standfirst: From 6 November, new offences will cover pornography depicting strangulation or suffocation, certain incest role-play and adults pretending to be children under 16. Campaigners welcome the move but say effective enforcement by platforms and regulators remains unresolved.

image.caption: The new rules cover pornography depicting strangulation or suffocation and certain forms of incest role-play.

sources.originalTitle: Porn showing choking or incest to be banned from early November, government says
Pornography with strangulation and incest to be banned in England and Wales next month
